questions.q: According to this lesson, what is the core skill behind professional chart design?
options: Adding a background image to every chart for branding
Always using as many colors as possible to make the chart eye-catching
Maximizing the number of gridlines for precision
Knowing what to take away, not just what to add
questions.explain: The lesson frames good design as a subtraction skill — removing anything that doesn't help the data communicate, rather than continuously adding decoration.

questions.q: In the before/after example, what did the 'before' chart include that added no data value?
options: A wood-grain background, a gray plot area, a redundant color legend, and heavy borders
A title describing the chart's contents
The bar chart's data labels
An axis showing the actual sales values
questions.explain: The cluttered version had decorative elements — background texture, unnecessary shading, a legend that duplicated the axis labels, and heavy borders — none of which changed or clarified the underlying data.

questions.q: In the 'after' version, why is only one bar shown in color while the rest are gray?
options: Because Tableau only allows one colored mark per chart
It was a rendering error in the original chart
Gray bars indicate missing data
To draw the reader's attention to the single most important data point without competing color everywhere
questions.explain: Reducing color to a single accent for the most important value, while the rest recede to gray, is a deliberate design choice to focus attention rather than an accident or limitation.

questions.q: What is the correct order of the clutter-removal sequence described in this lesson?
options: Reduce colors before removing any backgrounds
Add gridlines first, then add a legend, then add a background
There is no particular order — all steps happen at once
Remove backgrounds, remove redundant labels, reduce colors, then remove bolding and gridlines
questions.explain: The sequence moves from removing non-data backgrounds, to cutting labels that duplicate the axis or legend, to reducing color to a single accent, finishing with bolding and gridlines.

questions.q: Why does removing a redundant color legend make a chart clearer rather than less informative?
options: Because legends are never useful in any chart
Because Tableau requires legends to be hidden by default
Because the legend's information was already shown directly by the axis or category labels
Because removing the legend deletes the underlying data
questions.explain: When category names are already shown as axis labels, a separate color legend repeating the same names is redundant — removing it reduces clutter without losing information.
